subject: Life Skills & Future Readiness
title: One-Year Life Skills Academy: Learn. Lead. Impact.
tagline: A 50-week, Saturdays-only, project- and discussion-based journey building confident, ethical, future-ready young people — no written exams.

units.title: Welcome & Onboarding (start here, before Week 1)
units.summary: Meet the programme: its vision, values, how the year works, and the story that kicks it all off.

p: Welcome. Over the next year, every Saturday, you'll build the character, communication, thinking and future-readiness skills that no exam can fully measure — through real stories, live discussion and projects you actually create. There are no multiple-choice tests here. You are marked on showing up, thinking honestly, and building something real.
One live 60-minute session every Saturday for 50 weeks (one school year), organised into 4 quarters.
Each session opens with an icebreaker and reflection, moves into a real-world story and discussion, then a hands-on activity — never a lecture-only format.

Assessment is 100% project-, portfolio- and discussion-based: weekly participation + a portfolio you build all year + 3 Quarterly Capstones + 1 Grand Capstone Project at Week 50. There is no written exam and no 100-question test bank for this course.
You'll earn Bronze, Silver and Gold digital badges and fill a Future Ready Passport as you go.

To raise confident, ethical, emotionally intelligent and future-ready young people who can lead themselves, influence others positively, solve real-world problems and thrive in school, university, careers, entrepreneurship and life.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Tanmay Bakshi (18 years old) (Toronto, Canada)
p: Tanmay Bakshi spent his childhood playing with computers just like other kids played with building blocks. By the time he was just five years old, his dad taught him how to write very simple computer code. While his friends were playing video games, Tanmay was busy trying to understand how those video games actually worked under the hood. He did not want to just use technology; he wanted to build it.

When he was 11 years old, Tanmay heard about a brand new technology called Artificial Intelligence, or AI. Instead of waiting until he was an adult to learn it, he decided to start studying it right away. He ran into countless bugs and errors that made him want to pull his hair out. He often sat at his desk for hours, typing away and laughing at his own silly coding mistakes. But he kept adjusting his skills because he knew the world was changing fast, and he wanted to be ready for the future.

By the age of 15, major global tech companies noticed his unique skills. They invited him to speak on huge stages in front of thousands of adults to explain how the future of technology works. Tanmay proved that you do not have to wait until you grow up to prepare for the future. By starting early and learning the skills of tomorrow, anyone can become ready for whatever changes the world brings.

units.title: Week 1: Orientation: Becoming Future Ready
units.summary: Understand what 'future-ready' means and set a personal intention for the year ahead.

p: Icebreaker: 'If you could master one skill instantly, what would it be, and why?' Go around the room/call.
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Every year that changes the world starts the same way: with someone deciding, on an ordinary day, to stop waiting for permission to grow. That's the spirit behind this entire 50-week programme, and it's worth sitting with before diving into any single skill.

"Future-ready" doesn't mean predicting exactly what the world will look like in ten years — nobody can do that reliably. It means building a flexible toolkit of character, communication, thinking and technical instincts that hold up no matter which specific jobs, tools, or crises the future actually brings. The skills in this course — confidence, emotional intelligence, critical thinking, digital literacy, financial sense — have been useful in every decade of human history and will remain useful in whichever decade comes next.

Most school timetables are built around subjects that are easy to test, not necessarily the skills that determine how well a life goes. Confidence, resilience, and the ability to have a hard conversation calmly rarely appear on a report card, yet they quietly decide who thrives when things get difficult — in an exam hall, a job interview, or a friendship under strain.

A useful way to think about future-readiness is as six overlapping "pillars": Personal Excellence (knowing and managing yourself), Communication & Relationships, Leadership & Influence, Innovation & Problem Solving, Digital & AI Readiness, and Career & Financial Readiness. Nearly every week of this programme sits under one or more of these pillars, and by Week 50 you'll have touched all six directly.

Consider two students with identical grades. One has also learned to manage nerves before a presentation, ask for help without shame, and bounce back from a rejected university application. The other hasn't had the chance to practise any of that. On paper they look the same; in practice, the first student adapts faster to whatever life actually throws at them — which is the entire point of "future-ready."

This isn't about becoming a different person by Week 50. It's about noticing, one Saturday at a time, which of these six pillars already feels solid for you and which ones need deliberate practice — and then actually practising, since none of these skills improve just from hearing about them once.

ex.t: What 'starting early' looked like for Tanmay
b: Learned to code at age 5, years before it was 'expected'
Chose to study AI at 11, when almost no school offered it
Was invited to speak on global stages by 15 — because he had already been practising for a decade

p: Orientation is less a lesson and more a starting line. You don't need to have this figured out today — you need a direction, a reason to keep showing up on Saturdays for a year, and a first honest look at where you already are. That's what this session, and the letter you'll write to close it, are for.

units.title: Week 2: Growth Mindset
units.summary: Distinguish between a fixed and a growth mindset and practise reframing failure as feedback.

p: Icebreaker: Draw or describe your worst-ever first attempt at something you're now good at.
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Two students can fail the exact same test and walk away with completely different futures — not because of the grade itself, but because of the story each of them tells themselves about what that grade means.

Psychologist Carol Dweck's research on mindset identified two broad patterns in how people interpret difficulty. A fixed mindset treats ability as a fixed quantity you either have or don't — so failure feels like proof of a permanent limitation. A growth mindset treats ability as something built through effort and strategy — so failure becomes information about what to adjust next, not a verdict on your worth.

This isn't just a motivational slogan; it's grounded in how the brain actually works. Neuroplasticity — the brain's ability to form new neural connections — means that struggling productively with something hard is literally how skill gets built, the same way a muscle needs resistance to grow stronger. Avoiding difficulty to protect your ego also avoids the exact conditions that create improvement.

The language people use with themselves is a strong signal of which mindset is active in the moment. "I'm bad at maths" is a fixed-mindset sentence — it describes an unchangeable trait. "I haven't practised enough maths yet" is a growth-mindset sentence — it describes a temporary, fixable state. The word "yet" alone has been shown in classroom studies to shift how students respond to setbacks.

A growth mindset doesn't mean pretending failure feels good, or claiming anyone can achieve anything with enough positive thinking — that's a common misreading of the idea. It means treating a setback as data rather than a full stop: what specifically didn't work, and what's one adjustment worth trying next time? That question is available after every failure, no matter how discouraging the failure felt in the moment.

Growth mindset also shows up in how people respond to other people's success. A fixed mindset can feel threatened by someone else doing well, as if there's a limited amount of talent to go around. A growth mindset can admire and even learn from someone else's success, because ability isn't a zero-sum resource — someone else improving doesn't use up your own capacity to improve.

b: 'I can't do this' → 'I can't do this yet'
'I failed' → 'That attempt didn't work — what's next?'
'They're just naturally talented' → 'They've practised this longer than me'

p: Nobody arrives at Week 2 with a permanently fixed or permanently growth mindset — most people shift between the two depending on the day and the stakes. The goal this week isn't to eliminate every fixed-mindset thought forever; it's to notice one when it shows up, and practise swapping it for its growth-mindset version, deliberately, until that swap starts to feel more natural than automatic.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Kavinayan (12 years old) (Selangor, Malaysia)
p: Kavinayan stared at the screen during his online school session, and his face completely fell. His teacher had just announced a digital art contest for the whole school. Kavinayan loved drawing with pencils, but he had absolutely no idea how to use a digital tablet or art software. His first attempt on the tablet looked like a giant, messy blob of paint, and he accidentally deleted his entire project twice. He felt like throwing the tablet out the window.

Instead of quitting, Kavinayan decided to look at his messy blob and laugh. He told himself that his brain was just stretching to learn something new. He spent the next three weeks watching free internet videos, learning how to use the digital brushes, and practicing every single afternoon. Every time he made a mistake, he just smiled and hit the "undo" button.

When the day of the contest arrived, Kavinayan submitted a beautiful digital painting of a futuristic city. He did not win the first-place trophy, but he received a special award for the most creative design. He realized that talent is not something you are just born with. With a lot of practice and a willingness to laugh at your own mistakes, you can train your brain to learn absolutely anything.

What is the difference between 'I'm bad at this' and 'I'm not good at this yet'?
How did laughing at her mistakes help Kavinayan keep going?

Key takeaway: Distinguish between a fixed and a growth mindset and practise reframing failure as feedback.

units.title: Week 3: Knowing Yourself
units.summary: Identify personal strengths, values, and the causes that matter to you.

p: Icebreaker: Name three words other people would use to describe you — then three words you'd use for yourself.
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?
Ask most people to list three of their strengths and they hesitate — not because they lack strengths, but because almost nobody is ever asked to sit down and actually name them.

Self-knowledge has three practical components worth separating out: values (what actually matters to you, not what you're told should matter), strengths (what you do well, whether through natural aptitude or built-up practice), and triggers (what reliably frustrates, energises, or motivates you). Most people carry a vague sense of all three but have never written any of it down explicitly.

Frustration is one of the most underrated sources of self-knowledge. The things that genuinely annoy you — unfairness, waste, disorganisation, being talked over — usually point directly at a value you hold strongly, even if you've never named that value out loud. Marley Dias didn't set out to become an activist; she got frustrated by a bookshelf, and that frustration revealed exactly what she cared about.

Strengths aren't limited to talents you were simply born with. Some strengths are natural aptitudes (a quick memory, a calm voice), and others are built through repetition (patience with younger kids, staying organised under pressure) — both count, and the built kind is often more useful precisely because you know how you built it and can build more like it.

There's a difference between a strength and a personality label. "I'm a leader" is vague and hard to act on. "I naturally notice when a group discussion has stalled and ask a question to restart it" is specific, observable, and something you can actually get better at on purpose. The more specific your self-knowledge, the more useful it is.

Self-knowledge isn't static — it updates as you take on new experiences and notice new patterns. The version of yourself you describe in Week 3 is a starting draft, not a final verdict, and it's worth revisiting later in the programme (particularly at the Quarter 1 Capstone) to see what's changed.

b: 3 things I'm proud of doing
3 things that consistently frustrate me (these often point at values)
1 compliment I've received more than once

p: Knowing yourself isn't a soft, optional extra before the "real" skills start — it's the foundation nearly everything else in this programme builds on. Confidence, goal-setting, leadership style, even career exploration in Quarter 4, all work better when they're built on an honest, specific picture of who you actually are, not a generic idea of who you think you're supposed to be.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Marley Dias (11 years old) (New Jersey, USA)
p: Marley Dias loved to read books, but one afternoon she realized something that made her very frustrated. As she looked at her massive pile of school library books, she noticed that none of the characters looked like her or shared her background. All the stories were about white boys and their dogs. Marley went to her mother to complain about how annoying this was.

Her mother looked at her and asked a very important question: "What are you going to do about it?" Marley had to take a good look at herself to figure out what she truly cared about. She realized that she was a natural organizer, a loud talker, and someone who valued fairness deeply. Instead of trying to blend in or stay quiet, she decided to use her unique personality traits to make a real change.

Marley started a public drive called #1000BlackGirlBooks to find and collect stories where black girls were the main characters. Her funny, energetic videos online went viral, and she soon collected over 10,000 books for schools around the world. By taking the time to understand her own identity and strengths, Marley found her true voice and helped thousands of other kids do exactly the same.
What is something in the world around you that frustrates you the way the book pile frustrated Marley?
What are three strengths people say you have?
What would you start if you knew it could not fail?
Complete a short strengths inventory individually, then share one insight with a partner.
Key takeaway: Identify personal strengths, values, and the causes that matter to you.

units.title: Week 4: Building Confidence
units.summary: Build practical strategies for speaking and acting with confidence even when afraid.

p: Icebreaker: What is something you were once terrified of that no longer scares you? What changed?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Confidence is one of the most misunderstood words in the English language — most people picture someone who never feels afraid, when in fact almost every confident person you'll ever meet still feels the fear; they've just learned to act anyway.

Diana Zuleta's story makes the distinction clear: her hands still shook, her heart still raced — the fear didn't disappear. What changed was her willingness to keep showing up in front of small, safe audiences until the same fear became familiar enough to act through. Confidence, in other words, is a decision to act despite fear, not evidence that fear is gone.

Confidence is built the same way physical strength is built: through repeated, moderately uncomfortable repetitions, not through one dramatic breakthrough. Speaking up once in a small group discussion, then asking a question in a bigger group, then presenting for two minutes to people you know — each rep is slightly harder than the last, and each one makes the next one feel more familiar.

Preparation quietly does a huge amount of the work that people mistake for raw bravery. Knowing your material cold, practising your opening line until it's automatic, and understanding your own body language all remove sources of fear before you even start — which is why confident-looking people are very often just well-prepared people, not naturally fearless ones.

There's an important difference between confidence and arrogance that's worth naming directly. Confidence is a private, internal sense that you can handle a challenge, win or lose. Arrogance is an external performance aimed at proving superiority to other people. Confident people can say "I don't know" or "I got that wrong" without it threatening how they see themselves — arrogant people usually can't.

Confidence is also domain-specific before it becomes general. Someone can be deeply confident on a football pitch and terrified of public speaking, or completely at ease presenting but nervous meeting new people one-on-one. Building confidence in one specific area — through the small-reps approach above — doesn't automatically transfer everywhere, but it does build a track record you can point to when tackling a new area.

b: Speak up once in a small group discussion
Ask a question in front of the whole class
Present for 2 minutes to people you know
Present to strangers or a panel

p: By the end of this week, the goal isn't to feel zero fear the next time you have to speak up, present, or try something new — that's not really how confidence works. The goal is to have one small, specific, slightly uncomfortable rep behind you, so the next rep after that feels just a little more familiar than this one did.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Diana Zuleta (13 years old) (Panama City, Panama)
p: Diana Zuleta was terrified of speaking in public. Whenever her teacher called on her to read a paragraph out loud in class, Diana’s heart would beat like a bass drum. Her hands would shake so much that she would drop her papers, causing her classmates to giggle. She felt like she was the least confident person on the planet.

One day, her school announced a mandatory speech competition for all students. Diana wanted to hide in the bathroom. But her older brother gave her a funny piece of advice: "Just practice your speech in front of our pet dog, Max. He won't judge your accent!" Diana actually tried it. She stood in her living room, wearing a silly hat to make herself laugh, and gave her speech to the dog, who just wagged his tail.

Every day, Diana practiced standing tall and speaking clearly. On the day of the competition, she walked up to the microphone. Her knees felt like jelly, but she remembered her practice sessions with Max. She took a deep breath, smiled at the crowd, and delivered her speech perfectly. She did not win the top prize, but as she walked off the stage, she realized the shaking had stopped. She learned that confidence is not a magical power you are born with; it is like a muscle that grows every time you face your fears.
What is something that makes your 'heart beat like a bass drum' the way public speaking did for Diana?
What is one small, brave thing you could do this week?
How is confidence different from not being scared at all?

Key takeaway: Build practical strategies for speaking and acting with confidence even when afraid.

units.title: Week 5: Personal Values & Character
units.summary: Define personal values and explain how character shows up under pressure.
keyWords: Integrity when no one is watching

p: Icebreaker: Complete the sentence — 'I could never respect someone who...' What value does that reveal?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?
Character rarely gets tested when things are easy — it gets tested in the specific, inconvenient moment when doing the right thing costs you something: time, popularity, comfort, or an easy win.

Values only matter in practice if they show up in decisions, not just in conversation. It's easy to say you value honesty; it's harder to tell a friend an uncomfortable truth they need to hear, or admit a mistake when staying quiet would be easier and no one would ever find out. The gap between stated values and actual behaviour is where character either shows up or doesn't.

A useful exercise is naming your "non-negotiables" — the two or three lines you refuse to cross regardless of pressure, popularity, or convenience. Having these named in advance matters because in-the-moment pressure narrows thinking; people under social or time pressure very often make decisions they wouldn't defend calmly later. A pre-decided non-negotiable is much harder to talk yourself out of in the heat of the moment.

Character and reputation are related but not identical. Reputation is what other people believe about you based on what they've seen; character is who you actually are, including in moments nobody is watching. The two usually align over a long enough timeline — hidden character eventually leaks into visible behaviour — but they can diverge sharply in the short term, which is exactly why character matters more than reputation management.

Values can genuinely conflict with each other, which is part of why living by them is hard rather than simple. Loyalty to a friend can conflict with honesty, if the honest thing to say might hurt them. Ambition can conflict with rest. Naming your values doesn't remove these conflicts — it gives you a framework for reasoning through them deliberately instead of just going with whatever feels easiest in the moment.

Small, everyday decisions build character just as much as dramatic ones — arguably more, because there are so many more of them. Whether you hand in your best work or your fastest work, whether you speak up when a group is being unfair to someone, whether you follow through on a promise nobody would notice you breaking — these ordinary moments are where character is actually built, rep by rep.

ex.t: Values vs behaviour — spot the gap
b: Value: honesty → Behaviour: do I tell the full truth even when it's awkward?
Value: fairness → Behaviour: do I speak up when I see someone treated unfairly?
Value: excellence → Behaviour: do I hand in my best work, or my fastest work?

p: This week isn't about producing a perfect list of virtues to live up to — it's about naming, specifically and honestly, what you actually refuse to compromise on, so that when a real test shows up (and it will), you've already decided in advance which way you're going to go.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Nihal Raj (7 years old, known as "Kicha") (Kochi, Kerala, India)
p: Nihal Raj loved cooking more than anything else. He spent hours in the kitchen with his mother, learning how to mix ingredients and bake delicious treats. He even started his own online cooking video channel, where his funny jokes and bright smile made him a hit with viewers worldwide. Soon, a major American television show noticed his talent and invited him to fly to Hollywood to cook live on TV.

A massive company saw his video and offered to pay him thousands of dollars to use his recipes to sell unhealthy junk food to kids. Nihal and his parents sat down to talk about the offer. It was a huge amount of money for a young boy. But Nihal valued health and honesty. He knew that selling bad food to his young fans was wrong, even if it made him rich.

Nihal looked at the big check and politely said no. Instead, he chose to partner with companies that made healthy snacks for children. He even donated a portion of his video earnings to local charities that fed hungry kids in his hometown. By standing firm on his personal values, Nihal proved that good character and staying true to what is right is worth much more than a pile of money.

When has doing the right thing been the harder choice for you?
How do your values show up in ordinary, everyday decisions?
List your top 3 values, then write one recent moment where you lived up to (or fell short of) each.
Key takeaway: Define personal values and explain how character shows up under pressure.

units.title: Week 6: Goal Setting
units.summary: Set specific, measurable personal goals and break them into actionable steps.

p: Icebreaker: What's a goal you achieved that felt impossible when you first set it?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

"I want to do better" and "I will score 75% or higher on my next two maths tests by practising three times a week" are both statements about improvement — but only one of them can actually be acted on tomorrow morning.

A goal without specifics and a deadline is really just a wish — pleasant to say, but practically useless for guiding action. The SMART framework (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) forces a vague wish into something you can actually plan around: what exactly will be different, how will you know, is it realistically possible, does it connect to something that matters to you, and by when.

Long-range goals (a year, five years, ten years) give a sense of direction, but they're too distant to act on directly — you can't "do" a ten-year goal today. Milestones translate distant direction into near-term action: a five-year goal of studying abroad might break into a one-year milestone of researching three universities and improving a specific grade this term.

Goals that are entirely about outcomes ("win the competition") are riskier to build motivation around than goals that include the process ("practise my routine four times a week"), because outcomes often depend partly on factors outside your control — other competitors, judges, luck. Process goals stay within your control even when the final outcome doesn't go your way, which keeps motivation alive through setbacks.

Accountability meaningfully increases the odds a goal actually gets pursued rather than quietly forgotten within a few weeks. Telling someone else your goal, checking in with them on progress, or simply writing it somewhere visible all increase the psychological cost of quietly abandoning it — which is precisely why goals kept entirely private are so much easier to let slide.

Goals sometimes need revising, and that's not the same as failing at them. New information — an injury, a changed interest, a discovered talent — can reasonably change what a good goal looks like partway through the year. The skill isn't rigidly sticking to an original plan no matter what; it's noticing when a genuine update is needed versus when you're just looking for an excuse to quit.

b: Vague: 'Get fit' → SMART: 'Run 5km without stopping within 8 weeks, training 3x/week'
Vague: 'Do better at school' → SMART: 'Raise my Biology grade from a C to a B by the mid-term exam'

p: A goal you've actually written down, with a number and a date attached, behaves completely differently in your head than a goal you've only ever thought about vaguely. This week's task — turning a vague hope into one SMART goal with three milestones — is a small piece of paper that quietly does a lot of the work of actually getting there.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Yassine El Idrissi (15 years old) (Casablanca, Morocco)
p: Yassine El Idrissi had a huge dream: he wanted to build his very own working robot before he graduated high school. When he told his friends, they laughed and said he was dreaming too big because robot parts were expensive and complicated. Yassine felt discouraged, but he decided to break his massive dream down into much smaller, bite-sized goals.

He wrote a checklist in his notebook. His goal for the first month was simply to save enough pocket money to buy a single small motor. His goal for the second month was to learn how to wire that motor to a battery. He treated each small step like a level in a video game, celebrating with a little dance in his room whenever a wire finally worked.

It took Yassine fourteen months of slow, steady work. There were days when things broke, but because his daily goals were so small, he never felt completely overwhelmed. By December 2019, Yassine placed his creation on his desk, flipped the switch, and watched his small robot roll across the floor. He learned that no dream is too big if you have the patience to break it down into tiny, daily steps.

What is the very first, smallest step toward that goal?
Who could help hold you accountable this year?

units.title: Week 7: Time Management
units.summary: Apply basic time-management tools to balance school, rest, and personal goals.

p: Icebreaker: If you had one extra hour every day, what would you actually do with it?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Almost nobody runs out of hours in a day — what actually runs out is intentional decisions about how those hours get spent, which is why two people with identical schedules can end a week feeling completely differently about what they accomplished.

Most time problems are really prioritisation problems wearing a disguise. "I don't have time" often actually means "I haven't decided this is more important than the things currently filling my time," which is a much more useful (if less comfortable) way to think about it, because it puts the decision back in your hands rather than blaming an unchangeable shortage of hours.

Time-blocking — assigning specific hours on a calendar to specific tasks, rather than keeping an open-ended to-do list — tends to outperform to-do lists alone, because a list doesn't force you to be honest about how much time something actually takes or where it will actually fit. A block on a calendar has to compete for real space against everything else already scheduled.

Protecting focus sometimes requires actively saying no — to a scroll session, an extra commitment, or a "quick chat" that quietly becomes an hour. Every yes to something is, by definition, a no to something else, even if that trade-off isn't stated out loud. Getting comfortable saying no to smaller things is often what makes room for the things that actually matter.

Not all hours are equal in quality. Most people have a stretch of the day when focus comes more easily (often, though not always, earlier rather than later) and a stretch when focus is harder to sustain. Matching demanding tasks to high-focus hours, and easier tasks to low-focus hours, gets more done than treating every hour of the day as interchangeable.

Rest belongs inside a time-block plan, not outside it as an afterthought. Scheduling recovery — sleep, downtime, unstructured time — the same way you'd schedule homework protects it from being the first thing sacrificed when a week gets busy, which is exactly what tends to happen when rest is treated as optional rather than planned.

b: Mon–Fri 4–5pm: homework block (phone in another room)
Tue/Thu 6–6:30pm: skill practice (sport, instrument, coding)
Sat: this session + free/rest time
Sun evening: 15-min plan for the week ahead

p: A time-block schedule isn't a rigid cage — it's a first draft, and first drafts are meant to be adjusted once you see how the real week actually goes. The point of this week's challenge isn't a perfect plan on paper; it's the practice of deciding, on purpose, where your hours go instead of discovering afterward where they went.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Chloe Soh (14 years old) (Singapore)
p: Chloe Soh was a busy teenager. She played competitive badminton, took weekly piano lessons, and had a mountain of school homework every night. She was so stressed out that she kept forgetting her assignments, showing up late to sports practice, and staying up until midnight trying to finish her essays. Her life felt like a chaotic storm.

One evening, Chloe accidentally wore two different colored socks to badminton practice because she was in such a rush. Her teammates laughed, and Chloe realized she needed a better system. She decided to sit down and create a simple weekly time chart using bright, colorful markers. She blocked out exact times for studying, practicing piano, and playing sports, but she also made sure to schedule an hour just for relaxing and watching TV.

Chloe stuck the colorful chart right on her bedroom door. Whenever her friends asked her to hang out, she checked her chart first to see if she had free time. Within two weeks, Chloe stopped rushing. She was getting better grades, sleeping early, and she never wore mismatched socks to practice again. She learned that managing your time does not take away your freedom; it actually gives you your free time back.
What usually eats up your time without you noticing?
What is one task you keep postponing, and why?
How could a weekly plan change your Saturdays?
Draft a one-week time-block schedule for yourself using the categories above.
Key takeaway: Apply basic time-management tools to balance school, rest, and personal goals.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Build a one-week time-block schedule and try to follow it for the coming week.

units.title: Week 8: Emotional Intelligence I (Self-Awareness)
units.summary: Recognise and name your own emotions as they happen (self-awareness).

p: Icebreaker: On a scale of 1–5, how easy is it for you to name what you're feeling in the moment? Why?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Ask someone how they're feeling and "fine" is often the entire answer — not because nothing is happening emotionally, but because most people were never taught a vocabulary for what's actually going on underneath "fine."

Self-awareness — noticing what you're feeling and what triggered it, in real time rather than hours or days later — is widely considered the foundation of emotional intelligence, because you can't manage an emotion you haven't first noticed and named. Emotions themselves aren't good or bad; frustration, fear, and disappointment are all useful information, not problems to be eliminated.

Building an emotional vocabulary beyond "happy, sad, angry" changes how clearly you can think about what's happening. "Frustrated" is different from "overwhelmed." "Disappointed" is different from "embarrassed." A precise word points toward a precise cause and, often, a precise next step — a vague word like "bad" points toward nothing actionable at all.

A simple but well-studied technique called affect labelling — naming an emotion out loud or in writing ("I notice I'm feeling anxious about this presentation") — measurably reduces how intensely that emotion is experienced. This isn't a trick or a platitude; brain-imaging studies show that naming an emotion engages regions associated with regulation, calming the emotional response somewhat just through the act of naming it.

Triggers are worth tracking specifically, not just emotions in isolation. Two questions turn a vague feeling into useful data: where do I feel this in my body (tight chest, clenched jaw, restless legs), and what happened immediately before I started feeling this way? Patterns usually emerge after a few days of asking these questions honestly.

Self-awareness isn't about becoming emotionless or perfectly calm at all times — that's neither realistic nor actually desirable. It's about creating a small gap between feeling something and acting on it, so the feeling informs your next move instead of controlling it completely. That small gap is where almost all of emotional intelligence actually lives.

b: Beyond 'happy/sad/angry': frustrated, overwhelmed, disappointed, proud, nervous, relieved, embarrassed
Ask: where do I feel this in my body?
Ask: what happened right before I started feeling this way?

p: A three-day emotions diary sounds small, but it's often the first time anyone has been asked to track this deliberately rather than just letting feelings wash past unexamined. The patterns that show up — which situations, which times of day, which people — are the raw material for everything else emotional intelligence builds on, including this week's second half: empathy for others.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Juanito "Aries" Toledo (13 years old) (Cebu City, Philippines)
p: Juanito Toledo was usually a very happy student, but exam week always turned him into a completely different person. Whenever he sat down to take a math test, his throat would tighten, his palms would sweat, and he would snap angrily at anyone who tried to talk to him. He did not understand why a simple piece of paper made him feel so furious inside.

During one stressful test, Juanito dropped his eraser, and when his friend picked it up for him, Juanito yelled, "Leave me alone!" The teacher had to step in, and Juanito felt deeply embarrassed. He realized he needed to understand what was happening inside his own body. He began to notice that the anger always started with a heavy feeling in his stomach right before the test papers were handed out.

The next time he felt that heavy stomach feeling, Juanito did not ignore it. He stopped, closed his eyes, and whispered to himself: "I am not angry at my friends; I am just scared of failing this test." Simply naming the true feeling made the heavy weight in his stomach disappear. By learning to recognize his own emotions early, Juanito was able to stay calm, apologize to his friend, and pass his math test with a clear mind.
What emotion is hardest for you to name in the moment?
What usually triggers a strong reaction in you?
What helps you calm down when you feel overwhelmed?
Keep a 3-day emotions diary: one line per day naming a feeling and its trigger.
Key takeaway: Recognise and name your own emotions as they happen (self-awareness).
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Keep an emotions diary for three days, naming what you felt and what triggered it.

units.title: Week 9: Emotional Intelligence II (Empathy & Relationships)
units.summary: Practise empathy and read the emotions of others in relationships.

p: Icebreaker: Describe a time someone's kindness changed your day, even in a small way.
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Self-awareness looks inward; empathy looks outward — and the second skill only really works once the first one is in place, because it's hard to accurately read someone else's feelings if you're still confused about your own.

Empathy is the ability to notice and respond to what someone else is feeling, not just what they're literally saying — and it's genuinely a skill that improves with deliberate practice, not a fixed personality trait some people simply have and others don't. Richard Turere's story from later in this programme (Week 14) is really an empathy story as much as a listening one: he heard fear underneath anger.

Curiosity is the engine of empathy. Instead of assuming you already understand what someone is going through based on a quick read of the situation, genuine empathy starts from a question: "what might actually be going on for this person right now?" That small shift — from assumption to curiosity — changes how accurately you read other people, and how they experience being around you.

Open questions unlock more honest answers than closed ones. "You okay?" invites a one-word "yeah" almost by default. "How are you actually doing?" or "you've seemed a bit off today — what's going on?" invites a real answer, because it signals that you're genuinely asking rather than performing a social script.

Empathy has a cost that's worth naming honestly: consistently tuning into other people's emotional states takes energy, and without any boundaries it can tip into what's sometimes called compassion fatigue. Healthy empathy includes noticing your own limits, not just other people's needs — caring for others sustainably requires also looking after yourself.

Empathy doesn't require agreeing with someone or having gone through the identical experience yourself. You can empathise with a teammate's frustration about a decision you still think was right, or with a friend's grief over something you've never personally lost. Empathy is about understanding someone's emotional experience, not endorsing every conclusion they've drawn from it.

b: Notice a change in someone's usual behaviour
Ask an open question ('How are you actually doing?') instead of a closed one ('You okay?')
Listen to understand, not to reply

p: Checking in meaningfully with someone this week — really asking, and really listening to the answer — is a small act, but it's also exactly the skill that, practised over years, makes someone the kind of friend, teammate, or leader other people trust with the truth about how they're actually doing.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Thabo Ndlovu (15 years old) (Johannesburg, South Africa)
p: Thabo Ndlovu was the most popular guy in his class, and he loved to crack jokes to make his classmates laugh. One morning, a new student named David joined the class. David wore thick glasses, sat completely quietly in the back row, and spoke with a different accent. Thabo thought it would be funny to mimic David's voice during lunchtime, and all the other kids laughed along.

But as Thabo watched David walk away alone with his head down, he saw how tightly David was clutching his backpack. Thabo suddenly remembered how terrified he had felt when he changed schools two years before. He realized his jokes were not actually funny; they were just mean.

The next day, Thabo decided to use his social skills differently. He walked over to the back row and sat right next to David during lunch. He handed David an apple, smiled, and asked him how his first week was going. The other kids saw Thabo doing this and decided to come over to join them too. Thabo learned that true emotional intelligence is not about making people laugh at someone else; it is about putting yourself in another person's shoes and using your influence to lift them up.
When did someone's empathy really help you?
How can you tell when a friend is struggling, even if they don't say it?
What is one way you can check in on someone this week?
Identify someone who might be having a hard week and check in with them meaningfully before next session.
Key takeaway: Practise empathy and read the emotions of others in relationships.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Check in meaningfully with someone who seems to be having a hard week and note what you noticed.

units.title: Week 10: Building Positive Habits
units.summary: Design a positive daily habit using cues, routines, and rewards.

p: Icebreaker: What's one small habit you already have that you're proud of?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Nobody decides, once, to become a disciplined person and simply stays that way forever — discipline is built from small, repeated actions, and the mechanics of how those actions get repeated matter more than willpower alone.

Habits form through a predictable loop: a cue (something that triggers the behaviour), a routine (the behaviour itself), and a reward (the reason your brain wants to repeat it). Most habits that fail to stick were never actually designed — the cue and reward were left to chance, so the habit had nothing reliably prompting or reinforcing it.

Designing a habit on purpose means choosing a specific, existing cue to attach a new behaviour to, rather than relying on remembering. "After I brush my teeth, I do ten push-ups" is far more reliable than "I'll try to exercise sometime today," because the existing habit of brushing teeth becomes the trigger for the new one, borrowing a routine your brain already runs automatically.

Small, consistent habits compound in a way dramatic one-off efforts usually don't. A ten-minute habit repeated daily for a year adds up to roughly sixty hours of deliberate practice — far more than a handful of intense, unsustainable pushes that burn out after a week or two. Consistency beats intensity almost every time over a long enough timeline.

Visible tracking — a calendar with X's, a habit-tracking app, a simple checklist — works because it makes progress tangible and creates a small reward (not breaking the chain) separate from the habit's real long-term benefit, which is often too slow and abstract to feel motivating on its own in the early weeks.

Not every habit needs to be kept forever. Some habits are meant to build a specific skill and can be retired once that skill is established; others (like sleep or exercise habits) are worth sustaining indefinitely. Part of habit-building is periodically checking whether a habit is still serving its original purpose, or whether it's time to design a new one.

b: Cue: right after brushing teeth → Routine: 10 push-ups → Reward: check it off a visible tracker
Cue: opening a textbook → Routine: 25-minute focused study block → Reward: a short break/snack

p: One week of tracking a single habit won't transform anyone's life on its own — but it will teach you, concretely, how habit design actually works: a specific cue, a specific routine, a specific reward. That mechanical understanding is what makes every future habit, for the rest of this programme and beyond, easier to build on purpose rather than leaving to chance.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Lewis Pugh (13 years old) (Bristol, United Kingdom)
p: Lewis Pugh wanted to get into the best shape of his life so he could make the school football team. On New Year's Day, he came up with a massive plan: he was going to do 100 push-ups, run five miles, and eat only vegetables every single day. On day one, he did great. But by day three, his entire body was so sore that he could barely lift his arms, and he quit his new routine completely to eat chocolate on the couch.

Lewis realized his giant plan was a mistake. He decided to try a completely different approach called the "Tiny Habit Strategy." Instead of doing 100 push-ups, his new daily goal was to do just five push-ups right after he brushed his teeth in the morning. It was so incredibly easy that he couldn't find any excuse to skip it.

He did his five push-ups every single day for a month. Soon, five push-ups felt like nothing, so he naturally increased the number to ten, and then to fifteen. By the time the football tryouts arrived in September, Lewis was doing fifty push-ups easily every morning without even thinking about it. He proved that massive changes do not come from giant, exhausting efforts, but from small, positive actions repeated every single day until they become a natural habit.
What is one small habit that could make a big difference in your life?
What usually derails your good habits?
How could you redesign your environment to make a habit easier?
Pick one positive habit, define its cue and reward, and start a tracker for the week.
Key takeaway: Design a positive daily habit using cues, routines, and rewards.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Pick one positive habit and track it daily for a week using a simple habit tracker.

units.title: Week 11: Resilience & Overcoming Failure
units.summary: Build resilience strategies for bouncing back after failure or setback.

p: Icebreaker: Share a time you failed at something publicly. What did you do next?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Every impressive achievement anyone has ever pointed to as "talent" was, almost without exception, built on a pile of failed attempts nobody ever mentions — which is exactly why resilience matters more than avoiding failure ever could.

Gitanjali Rao's water-testing device went through prototype after failed prototype before it worked reliably enough to win recognition. Each failure wasn't a detour from the real work — it was the real work, the process by which a rough idea becomes a working solution. Treating failed attempts as wasted time misunderstands how almost all real achievement actually happens.

Resilience isn't about not falling — everyone falls, repeatedly, at almost everything worth doing. Resilience is about the speed and quality of getting back up: how long it takes to move from disappointment to a next useful step, and whether that next step is thoughtful or just an attempt to feel better in the moment.

A simple three-question routine turns a setback into something usable rather than something purely painful: what actually happened, in plain facts rather than catastrophised interpretation? What's one specific thing this taught me? What's my very next concrete step? Skipping straight to "what's my next step" without the first two questions often means repeating the same mistake.

Resilience is helped enormously by social support, and this is worth stating plainly because independence is sometimes wrongly treated as the mark of true resilience. Asking for help after a setback — from a friend, a teacher, a mentor — isn't a failure of resilience; reaching out effectively when you're struggling is itself a resilience skill, arguably one of the most important ones.

There's a real difference between healthy resilience and simply grinding through pain without adjustment. Resilience includes the willingness to change approach when something genuinely isn't working — continuing to do the exact same thing that already failed, purely out of stubbornness, isn't resilience, it's just repetition. Resilient people adapt the plan while keeping the underlying goal.

b: 'I failed the test' → 'This test showed me exactly which topics to revise'
'I lost the match' → 'This match showed me what to train next'

p: Writing honestly about a real past failure — not a humble-brag disguised as a failure story, but something that actually stung — and naming one lesson still in use today is this week's task precisely because resilience is best understood by examining a real example from your own life, not just discussing the concept in the abstract.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Gitanjali Rao (10 years old) (Lone Tree, Colorado, USA)
p: Gitanjali Rao was watching the news with her parents when she learned about a terrible crisis in Flint, Michigan. The city's drinking water was contaminated with dangerous chemicals, and thousands of young kids were getting sick from drinking it. Gitanjali felt a deep urge to help, so she decided to invent a cheap, fast device that could test water safety instantly.

She spent months working on her invention in her family's kitchen, using a small computer chip and various sensors. But nothing worked on the first try. Her device failed to turn on twenty times in a row, and her sensors kept giving completely incorrect readings. Gitanjali felt frustrated and wondered if she was simply too young to solve such a massive adult problem.

Instead of throwing her broken prototype in the trash, Gitanjali treated each failure like a valuable clue. She reached out to clean-water scientists online, fixed her messy wiring mistakes, and kept testing her device over and over again. After two years of constant failures and adjustments, her device, which she named Tethys, worked perfectly. At age 12, she won the title of "America’s Top Young Scientist." Gitanjali showed the world that failure is not the opposite of success; it is just a necessary step on the road to getting things right.
Gitanjali failed many prototypes before succeeding — what does that tell you about failure?
Describe a setback you experienced and what you learned from it.
What helps you get back up after disappointment?
Write about a real setback and identify one lesson from it that you still use today.
Key takeaway: Build resilience strategies for bouncing back after failure or setback.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Write about a past failure and identify one lesson it taught you that you still use today.

p: Icebreaker: In one sentence, what's the biggest thing you've realised about yourself this quarter?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?
Eleven Saturdays of building character, confidence, and personal effectiveness all lead here — not to a written test, but to a presentation of real evidence of who you've become since Week 1.

"My Future Blueprint" asks for five specific pieces of evidence rather than a single generic reflection: a Personal Vision Board, your 1/5/10-year goals from Week 6, a Strength Assessment drawing on Week 3's self-knowledge work, a Habit Tracker from Week 10, and a Personal Growth Plan that honestly names where you're headed next.

A strong capstone presentation connects these five pieces into one coherent story, rather than presenting five disconnected worksheets. The strongest presentations show how a value named in Week 5, a goal set in Week 6, and a habit tracked in Week 10 are all actually pointing in the same direction — that coherence is what separates a genuine reflection from a checklist.

Judges and facilitators are specifically looking for evidence of real reflection, not just completed forms — specific goals rather than vague ones, honest acknowledgment of what hasn't gone well alongside what has, and a growth plan for the next quarter that's genuinely believable and doable, not just impressively ambitious on paper.

This capstone is also a natural moment to revisit the self-knowledge work from Week 3. The version of yourself you described in that early session was a first draft — eleven weeks later is a good moment to ask honestly what's changed, what's been confirmed, and what you'd now describe differently.

The awards recognised today — Best Personal Growth, Most Improved Student, Best Reflection Journal, Best Goal Planner, Confidence Champion — deliberately reward different kinds of progress, not just the single most polished presentation. Growth from a difficult starting point counts as much here as a strong final result.
