units.title: Week 13: Communication Fundamentals
units.summary: Apply the principle of simple, clear, and direct communication.

p: Icebreaker: Retell a piece of news in exactly one sentence.
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Joshua Williams' three-page speech about global hunger statistics lost a grocery store manager's attention within the first minute — his single honest sentence about fifty hungry kids next door won a donation on the spot. The gap between those two moments is the entire lesson of this week.

Clear communication is not about sounding impressive — it's about being understood, quickly and completely, by the actual person in front of you. Long words and complicated sentences very often signal that the speaker hasn't fully worked out their own point yet, not that the point itself requires complexity. Genuinely clear thinkers tend to produce genuinely simple sentences.

A practical test before speaking or writing anything important: could a ten-year-old follow this? If the honest answer is no, the issue usually isn't that the topic is inherently complicated — it's that the explanation hasn't been simplified enough yet. Almost any idea, however sophisticated, can be explained in plain language once it's genuinely understood.

Audience awareness is what separates good communicators from merely articulate ones. The same piece of information needs a different shape depending on who's receiving it — a grocery store manager with two minutes needs a different opening than a classroom with an hour. Communication that ignores the listener's time, context, and priorities, however accurate, tends to fail.

Filler words, jargon, and unnecessary qualifiers ("sort of," "basically," "I would say that potentially") quietly bury the actual message under noise. Cutting them isn't about sounding robotic — it's about making sure the listener's attention lands on the point that matters, rather than being spent decoding padding around it.

Clear communication also requires knowing your own single main point before you open your mouth. Joshua's turning point came the moment he stopped reading his prepared notes and said, in effect, one clear sentence: here's the need, here's the ask. Most communication failures trace back to the speaker trying to say three things at once instead of committing to one.

b: 'We are experiencing a significant deficit in nutritional resources' → 'We need food'
'I would appreciate the opportunity to elaborate' → 'Can I explain?'

p: Explaining something you know well in thirty seconds, using only simple words, is a genuinely useful discipline — not because brevity is always better, but because the exercise forces you to find the one sentence that actually matters, which is exactly the skill Joshua discovered he needed in that grocery store meeting.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Joshua Williams (17 years old) (Miami, Florida, USA)
p: Joshua Williams ran a foundation that collected food for families in need. He had a big meeting with a grocery store manager to ask for a donation of one hundred boxes of cereal. Joshua was nervous, so he wrote a long, three-page speech. During the meeting, he started reading his papers, talking very fast about global hunger facts, and using complicated business words he found online.

The manager looked confused and kept checking his watch. Joshua realized he was losing his audience. He stopped reading, took a breath, and decided to simplify his message. He laughed at himself, closed his notebook, and said, "Sir, to be simple, we have fifty hungry kids in the neighborhood next door who need breakfast this Saturday. Can you help us feed them?"

The manager’s face instantly changed. He smiled and said, "Yes, absolutely." Joshua learned that good communication is not about using big words or giving long speeches. It is about keeping your message simple, clear, and direct so the other person can easily understand how to help.
Why did Joshua's long speech fail where his simple sentence worked?
What is a time you over-explained something that should have been simple?
How would you explain your favourite hobby in one sentence to a stranger?
Explain a topic you know well to a partner in under 30 seconds, using only simple words.
Key takeaway: Apply the principle of simple, clear, and direct communication.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Deliver a speech to your family and ask them to score you on clarity.

units.title: Week 14: Active Listening
units.summary: Practise active listening techniques that go beyond hearing words.
keyWords: Listening for feeling, not just facts

p: Icebreaker: Pair up. One person talks for 60 seconds about their weekend; the other may not speak at all — only listen.
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Richard Turere walked into a room full of angry village elders ready to explain his clever invention — and the single most useful thing he did was stay quiet long enough to hear what they were actually afraid of.

Active listening means giving genuinely full attention: no phone, no rehearsing your next sentence while the other person is still talking, no interrupting to correct a small detail before the larger point has landed. It sounds simple, but most everyday conversation is actually two people alternately talking, not two people alternately listening.

Listening for feeling, not just content, is what separates active listening from merely hearing words. Richard's breakthrough wasn't about the words the elders used — it was noticing that their anger about cattle was really fear about children walking to school in the dark. The stated complaint and the real concern underneath it were two different things.

Simple, physical active-listening moves make a measurable difference: nodding, brief verbal encouragers like "go on" or "I see," and reflecting back what you heard ("so what you're saying is...") before responding with your own view. These small signals tell the other person they've actually been heard, which changes how openly they continue talking.

Active listening doesn't mean agreeing with everything you hear, or staying silent forever without contributing your own view. It means fully understanding a position before responding to it — which, counterintuitively, often makes your eventual response more persuasive, because it directly addresses what the other person actually said rather than a version you assumed they meant.

One of the most common listening failures is "listening to respond" rather than "listening to understand" — spending someone else's talking time mentally drafting your reply instead of actually processing what they're saying. This habit is extremely common and mostly invisible to the person doing it, which is exactly why it's worth deliberately noticing and correcting.

b: Put the phone away, face the speaker
Don't plan your reply while they're still talking
Reflect back what you heard before adding your own point

p: Practising active listening with three different people this week, and writing down what you actually noticed, turns a concept you've just read about into a skill you've actually tried — and most people are surprised by how much they usually miss when they're only half-listening.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Richard Turere (21 years old) (Kitengela, Kenya)
p: Richard Turere grew up protecting his family's cows from lions. When he was younger, he invented "Lion Lights"—a system of flashing lights that kept predators away. Because of his cool invention, he was invited to help a nearby community where lions were still attacking livestock. In the first meeting, the village elders were angry and shouting. Richard wanted to interrupt them immediately to explain how smart his technology was.

Instead, Richard chose to keep his mouth shut and listen with his eyes and ears. He did not look at his phone or think about his next sentence. He noticed that the elders were not just mad about the cows; they were actually terrified for the safety of their children who walked to school in the dark.

Because Richard listened to their deeper fears, he did not just install lights around the cow pens. He also put lights along the dark school paths. The elders were amazed and thanked him warmly. Richard realized that active listening means hearing what people are feeling, not just the words they are saying.
What did Richard hear that the words alone did not say?
When was the last time you felt truly listened to?
What gets in the way of your listening fully to someone?
Practise active listening with three different people this week and record what you noticed.
Key takeaway: Practise active listening techniques that go beyond hearing words.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Practice active listening with three people during the week and record what you learned.

units.title: Week 15: Public Speaking
units.summary: Deliver a short speech with presence, eye contact, and authenticity.
keyWords: Speaking from the heart vs reading a script

p: Icebreaker: In 30 seconds, without notes, tell the group about your favourite meal.
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Marinel Ubaldo stood in front of hundreds of world leaders with sweating hands and a genuine urge to run back to her seat — and delivered one of the more memorable speeches of that conference anyway, because she chose to speak from her own experience instead of reading a script.

Public speaking anxiety is close to universal — surveys consistently rank it among people's most common fears, ahead of many things that are objectively more dangerous. The goal isn't eliminating nerves entirely (which very few speakers, even professional ones, ever fully achieve); it's speaking clearly and connecting with an audience despite the nerves still being present.

A strong short talk generally has three anchors: a strong opening line that earns attention in the first few seconds, one clear central message rather than several competing ones, and eye contact with the actual room rather than a fixed point on your notes. Trying to cover too many points is one of the most common ways a talk loses its audience.

Speaking from genuine experience, rather than reciting memorised facts, tends to land more powerfully with an audience — which is exactly what shifted the room for Marinel. Facts inform an audience; a real story, told honestly, moves them. The strongest talks usually combine both, but lead with the human element.

Physical preparation matters as much as content preparation. Slow, deliberate breathing before speaking calms the physiological signs of anxiety (racing heart, shallow breath) that otherwise bleed into a shaky voice. Standing with weight evenly balanced, rather than shifting nervously, also signals — both to the audience and to your own nervous system — that you're in control.

Every speaker, however experienced, has moments mid-talk where a thought disappears or a word doesn't come. A brief pause to gather yourself reads as composed to an audience, even though it can feel like an eternity to the speaker in the moment. Treating a pause as a tool rather than a disaster changes how recoverable these moments feel.

b: Opening: a question or a short story hook
Middle: one main point, with one example
Closing: what you want the audience to remember or do

p: Delivering a two-minute unscripted talk on something you genuinely care about — not something you think sounds impressive, but something you actually have a real opinion on — is this week's practice, because Marinel's story only works as a lesson once you've felt, even briefly, the same nerves she had to speak through.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Marinel Ubaldo (22 years old) (Tacloban, Philippines)
p: Marinel Ubaldo was invited to speak at a massive global conference about climate change. She had to stand on a stage in front of hundreds of world leaders and television cameras. As she walked up to the microphone, she felt completely terrified. Her hands were sweating, and she thought about running back to her seat.

She looked out at the audience of adults in expensive suits. She realized that if she spoke in a boring, robotic voice, they would ignore her. She smiled, took a deep breath, and stood up straight. Instead of reading from a script, she looked directly into their eyes and spoke loudly and clearly from her heart about her home village.

The crowd sat in total silence, listening to every single word. When she finished, the entire room stood up to cheer. Marinel learned that public speaking is not about being a perfect actor. It is about standing tall, speaking clearly, and having the courage to share your true message with the world.
What made Marinel's speech land with world leaders, when a 'perfect' script might not have?
What topic could you speak passionately about for two minutes, unscripted?
What is your biggest fear about public speaking, and where does it come from?
Prepare and deliver a 2-minute unscripted talk on something you genuinely care about.
Key takeaway: Deliver a short speech with presence, eye contact, and authenticity.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Prepare and deliver a 2-minute unscripted talk on a topic you care about to the group.

units.title: Week 16: Storytelling
units.summary: Use storytelling structure (setup, challenge, resolution) to make a message memorable.

p: Icebreaker: What's a story (a film, a book, a family story) that has stuck with you for years? Why that one?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

A list of five facts about a topic is forgettable within a day; a story built around those same five facts can stay with someone for years — which is precisely why storytelling is one of the oldest and most reliable communication tools humans have.

A good story has a recognisable shape: a setup that establishes who and where, a challenge or turning point that creates tension, and a resolution that reveals what changed or what was learned. This structure isn't a rigid formula to follow mechanically — it's a pattern that shows up naturally in almost every memorable story, because human attention responds to it.

Specific detail is what makes a story land, and vague generalities are what make one forgettable. "I was nervous before the competition" is forgettable. "My hands were shaking so badly I dropped my water bottle backstage, twice" is a detail an audience can actually picture, and picturing something is what makes it memorable.

You don't need a dramatic life event to tell a genuinely good story. An ordinary moment — a small mistake, an awkward conversation, a quiet realisation — told honestly and with real detail, is often more powerful than an exaggerated or borrowed story, because audiences can generally sense the difference between something authentic and something performed.

Every good story earns its ending by connecting back to a lesson or a change, explicitly or implicitly. A story that just describes events without ever landing on what it meant leaves an audience wondering why they were told it. The resolution doesn't need to be stated as a moral lesson out loud — but the storyteller needs to know what it is.

Storytelling and honesty aren't in tension — the most effective personal stories are also the truest ones, because authentic detail is very hard to fake convincingly and audiences are generally better at detecting exaggeration than storytellers assume. Better to tell a smaller true story well than a bigger invented one unconvincingly.

b: Setup: 'I used to be terrified of...'
Challenge: 'Then this happened...'
Resolution: 'What I learned was...'

p: Writing and telling a genuine three-minute personal story — with a real beginning, a real challenge, and a real lesson — is harder than it sounds precisely because it asks for honesty rather than performance, which is exactly the skill that makes a story worth remembering after this session ends.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Htet Myet Aung (16 years old) (Yangon, Myanmar)
p: Htet Myet Aung wanted to convince his school principal to start a plastic recycling club. He gathered a huge pile of papers filled with charts, percentages, and scientific data about plastic trash. He gave a presentation to the principal, listing fact after fact. The principal just nodded politely but said the school did not have the budget for a new club.

Htet realized that dry facts were not enough to make people care. The next day, he asked to speak to the principal again. This time, he did not bring any charts. Instead, he told a story about a stray dog that lived near the school yard that got its muzzle stuck in a plastic snack bag that morning. He described how the students had to work together to carefully cut the bag off to save the frightened animal.

The principal's eyes widened, and he looked genuinely touched. He immediately approved the recycling club. Htet learned that while data is important, a good story connects with people's emotions and inspires them to take action.
What makes a story easy to remember compared to a list of facts?
What personal story could you tell that carries a lesson for others?
How is a good story different from just a list of events?
Write and tell a 3-minute personal story with a clear beginning, challenge and lesson.
Key takeaway: Use storytelling structure (setup, challenge, resolution) to make a message memorable.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Write and tell a 3-minute personal story with a clear beginning, challenge, and lesson.

units.title: Week 17: Body Language
units.summary: Read and use body language to strengthen (not undercut) a spoken message.

p: Icebreaker: Without speaking, use only your body to show 'I'm excited' — then 'I'm bored.'
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?
Words carry only part of any message — posture, gesture, eye contact and facial expression often communicate louder than what's actually being said, sometimes even directly contradicting it.

Body language works alongside spoken words in two directions: it can reinforce a message (open posture supporting a confident statement) or quietly undercut it (crossed arms and a frown undermining an otherwise well-written speech). Audiences pick up on this mismatch even when they can't articulate exactly what felt off.

Closed body language — crossed arms, eyes down, weight shifting from foot to foot — tends to read as defensive or nervous, regardless of what's actually being said. Open body language — shoulders back, steady (not staring) eye contact, purposeful rather than fidgety gestures — tends to read as confident and trustworthy, even when the speaker still feels nervous underneath.

Hand gestures, used naturally rather than mechanically, help an audience track and remember key points — research on communication consistently finds that speakers who gesture are perceived as more engaging and are better remembered than speakers who keep their hands still throughout. Gesturing isn't a distraction from the message; done naturally, it supports it.

Eye contact across an entire room, rather than fixating on one friendly face or one intimidating face, keeps an audience feeling individually addressed. A common beginner mistake is either avoiding eye contact entirely (reading as evasive) or locking onto a single point (reading as either overly intense or disconnected from everyone else in the room).

Body language can be practised and deliberately adjusted, the same way vocabulary or content can — it isn't a fixed personality trait some people simply have and others don't. Recording yourself delivering the same short statement with closed versus open posture, and comparing how each version feels and looks, makes the difference concrete rather than abstract.

b: Closed: arms crossed, eyes down, shifting weight → reads as defensive or nervous
Open: shoulders back, steady eye contact, purposeful gestures → reads as confident and trustworthy

p: Delivering the same thirty-second statement twice — once closed off, once open — and discussing the difference as a group turns an abstract idea about body language into something you can actually see and feel, which is far more convincing than simply being told that posture matters.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Kokona Hiraki (12 years old) (Tokyo, Japan)
p: Kokona Hiraki was the youngest skateboarder at the Tokyo Olympic Games. Before her final run, she was incredibly nervous. She noticed that some of her older competitors were standing with their arms crossed, looking down at the floor, and frowning. Their bodies looked tight and full of fear.

Kokona decided to use her body language to change her mindset. She stood up perfectly straight, put her hands on her hips like a superhero, and forced a big smile onto her face, even though she was trembling inside. She gave her coach a high-five and walked onto the skatepark with her head held high.

Her open and confident posture helped her body relax, and she pulled off an amazing performance to win the silver medal. Kokona proved that your body language does not just show others how you feel—it actually tells your own brain to be brave and confident.
What does closed-off body language communicate, even when the words are positive?
When have you 'read the room' through body language alone?
What is one body-language habit you want to change?
Deliver the same 30-second statement twice — once with closed posture, once open — and discuss the difference as a group.
Key takeaway: Read and use body language to strengthen (not undercut) a spoken message.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Practice a short presentation twice — once with closed posture, once open — and compare how it felt.

units.title: Week 18: Teamwork
units.summary: Contribute effectively to a team and value diverse roles within it.

p: Icebreaker: Name a team (sports, school, family) you were proud to be part of. What made it work?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

A team is not simply a group of individuals working near each other — it's a group that has figured out how their different strengths fit together toward one shared goal, which is a skill in itself, not an automatic result of putting people in the same room.

Strong teams generally share three things: a clear common goal everyone actually understands the same way, clear roles so effort isn't duplicated or left undone, and enough mutual respect that disagreement doesn't automatically become personal conflict. Teams missing any one of these three tend to struggle even when every individual member is talented.

Different team roles tend to recur across almost any group project: the Organiser who tracks tasks and deadlines, the Idea Generator who pushes for new angles, the Encourager who keeps morale up when things get hard, and the Finisher who makes sure things actually get completed rather than left at eighty percent. Most people naturally lean toward one or two of these.

Working well with people who think differently from you is a genuine skill, not something that either comes naturally or doesn't. It requires deliberately valuing a different approach rather than assuming your own instinct is automatically correct — which is uncomfortable at first, since it means sometimes being persuaded by someone whose thinking style feels unfamiliar.

Teams that are too similar — everyone with the same strengths, the same blind spots, the same instincts — often struggle in ways that aren't obvious until a problem hits exactly that shared blind spot. Diversity of thinking style within a team isn't just a nice-to-have; it's a practical safeguard against everyone missing the same thing.

Trust is built through small, reliable actions over time — doing what you said you'd do, admitting when you've fallen behind rather than hiding it, giving credit rather than claiming it. Trust built this way tends to hold up under pressure; trust that's only ever been declared verbally, without being tested by small actions, often doesn't.

b: The Organiser — keeps track of tasks and deadlines
The Idea Generator — pushes for new angles
The Encourager — keeps morale up
The Finisher — makes sure things actually get done

p: Working with someone you don't normally partner with, even on a small task, deliberately puts you outside a comfortable, familiar team dynamic — which is exactly the situation where the skill of genuine teamwork, rather than just familiarity with specific people, actually gets tested and built.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Precious, Blessing, and Favour (15-16 years old) (Lagos, Nigeria)
p: Three high school girls entered a tech competition to build a mobile app that could locate clean drinking water sources. At first, their teamwork was a complete disaster. Precious wanted to do all the coding herself, Blessing wanted to handle all the design, and Favour thought her own ideas were the only ones that made sense. They spent their first week arguing and got absolutely zero work done.

Their school mentor noticed the chaos and made them play a funny game: they had to tie their ankles together and try to walk across the room. Every time someone tried to run ahead, they all fell over laughing. They realized that a team cannot move forward if everyone is pulling in different directions.

They sat down and divided the work based on their specific strengths, promising to listen to each other's feedback without getting upset. By working together smoothly, they finished their app on time and won the regional tech prize. They learned that real teamwork means combining your different talents to achieve a goal that no one could reach alone.
What role do you naturally take on in a team — organiser, encourager, doer, ideas person?
Describe a team you were proud to be part of. What made it work?
What makes a team fall apart?
Work with someone you don't normally work with on a short task, then reflect on the experience.
Key takeaway: Contribute effectively to a team and value diverse roles within it.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Work with someone you don't normally work with on a small task and reflect on the experience.

units.title: Week 19: Conflict Resolution
units.summary: Apply a structured approach to resolving conflict calmly and fairly.
keyWords: Separating the person from the problem

p: Icebreaker: What's your instinctive first reaction when conflict starts — fight, avoid, or try to fix it?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Conflict itself isn't the problem most people assume it is — avoided conflict and badly handled conflict are what actually damage relationships; conflict that's addressed directly and respectfully often leaves a relationship stronger than before.

A useful principle in resolving disagreement is separating the person from the problem — addressing what happened and its effect, rather than making a character judgment about the other person. "This deadline was missed and it affected the whole group" is a problem statement; "you're unreliable" is a character attack, and the second one almost always triggers defensiveness rather than resolution.

A simple structure keeps difficult conversations productive: state the fact ("here's what I noticed"), state the effect ("here's how it affected me or the group"), then make a request rather than a demand ("here's what I'd like to happen next"). This structure keeps the conversation about the specific situation rather than escalating into a broader argument about character or history.

Most everyday conflict isn't actually about winning — it's about finding an outcome both people can genuinely live with. Framing a disagreement as something to "win" tends to produce a result where one person loses and quietly resents it, which usually resurfaces later in a different form rather than actually being resolved.

Listening for the other side's real concern, before responding with your own view, often reveals that a conflict looks smaller or more solvable than it first appeared. Two people arguing loudly about a schedule might actually both want the same underlying thing — to feel their time is respected — which is a much easier problem to solve together than it first seemed.

Timing matters in conflict resolution as much as wording does. A disagreement raised the moment emotions are highest — mid-argument, immediately after a frustrating event — is far harder to resolve calmly than the same disagreement raised once both people have had a short amount of time to cool down, without waiting so long that the issue festers unspoken.

b: 'Here's what I noticed...' (fact, not blame)
'Here's how it affected me...' (feeling)
'Here's what I'd like to happen next...' (request, not demand)

p: Role-playing a disagreement with a partner, using the fact-effect-request structure above, turns an abstract idea into muscle memory — so that the next time a real disagreement shows up, there's already a practised structure available instead of only raw emotion in the moment.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Jordan and Taylor (14 years old) (Chicago, Illinois, USA)
p: Jordan and Taylor were the co-captains of their school's science fair project. Two days before the deadline, they got into a massive argument. Jordan wanted to paint their display board bright blue, while Taylor insisted it should be neon green. They started shouting at each other, calling each other stubborn, and both threatened to quit the project completely.

Their science teacher stepped in before things got worse. She told them they could not talk about colors for five minutes. Instead, they had to answer one question: "What is the goal of this board?" Both boys admitted they just wanted the judges to read their text clearly.

Jordan realized neon green was too bright to read, and Taylor realized dark blue was too boring. They calmed down, stopped attacking each other's personalities, and decided to compromise by using a clean, light grey background with neat black letters. They resolved the conflict by focusing on the actual problem instead of their anger, and their project received a perfect score.
What is your instinctive reaction when conflict starts — fight, avoid, or fix?
Describe a conflict that was resolved well. What made it work?
How can disagreement actually make a team stronger?
Role-play a disagreement with a partner and practise resolving it using the script above.
Key takeaway: Apply a structured approach to resolving conflict calmly and fairly.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Role-play a disagreement with a partner and practise resolving it using a calm, structured approach.

units.title: Week 20: Negotiation
units.summary: Practise basic negotiation to reach mutually beneficial outcomes.

p: Icebreaker: What's something you successfully negotiated recently, even a small thing?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Negotiation has an image problem — many people picture pressure tactics and someone trying to "win" at another's expense, when the most effective negotiators actually spend most of their time listening for what the other side genuinely needs.

The distinction between positions and interests is central to effective negotiation. A position is what someone says they want ("I want a later curfew"); an interest is the underlying need behind that request ("I want to be trusted with more independence"). Arguing over positions tends to produce a stalemate; understanding the interest underneath often opens up compromises neither side had considered.

Preparation changes negotiation outcomes more than most people expect. Knowing clearly what you want, why you want it, and what you'd genuinely be willing to trade in return — before the conversation starts — puts you in a far stronger position than improvising in the moment, when it's easy to either concede too quickly or dig in too rigidly.

Good negotiators generally listen more than they talk, especially early in a conversation. It's genuinely difficult to propose a compromise that actually works for the other person if you don't yet understand what they actually need — which is why negotiation, done well, often looks less like arguing and more like a structured conversation aimed at understanding first.

Framing a request around mutual benefit, rather than purely personal gain, tends to land better than framing it as a demand. "If I show I can manage a later curfew responsibly for a month, could we revisit it?" invites collaboration; "I deserve a later curfew" invites resistance, even if the underlying request is essentially the same.

Not every negotiation should end in a deal, and knowing when to walk away or postpone is itself part of the skill. Agreeing to something just to end an uncomfortable conversation often creates a worse outcome than taking more time to find an arrangement that genuinely works for both sides.

b: Position: 'I want a later curfew' → Interest underneath: 'I want to be trusted with more independence'
Naming the real interest often opens up more creative compromises than arguing over the position

p: Negotiating one real, small decision at home this week — rather than just discussing negotiation in the abstract — is where the difference between positions and interests actually becomes useful, turning a classroom concept into something you've genuinely practised on a decision that matters to you.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Aarav Mehta (15 years old) (Mumbai, India)
p: Aarav wanted his school to allow students to wear casual clothes on Fridays instead of their strict school uniforms. He went to the principal’s office and demanded the change, saying uniforms were boring. The principal immediately said no, explaining that uniforms keep the school looking neat and disciplined.

Aarav realized that demanding things never works in a negotiation. He had to think about what the principal cared about. He went back to his classmates and proposed a deal. He returned to the principal with a polite plan: "If we wear casual clothes on Fridays, every student will pay a small fee, and we will donate all that money to a local children's hospital. Plus, we promise no torn or inappropriate clothing."

The principal smiled. He saw that Aarav’s plan maintained school discipline while helping a great cause. He agreed to the deal. Aarav learned that negotiation is not about winning an argument; it is about finding a smart solution where both sides get something they want.
What is the difference between negotiating to 'win' and negotiating for a fair outcome?
Describe a time you negotiated for something — with a parent, teacher, or friend.
What would you need to prepare before an important negotiation?
Negotiate a real, small decision at home this week and reflect on how it went.
Key takeaway: Practise basic negotiation to reach mutually beneficial outcomes.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Negotiate a real, small decision at home this week (e.g. a curfew or a chore split) and reflect on the outcome.

units.title: Week 21: Leadership Through Service
units.summary: Understand leadership as service to others, not authority over them.

p: Icebreaker: Name someone who leads without having an official title. What makes them a leader anyway?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Leadership doesn't require a title, an election, or anyone's official permission — it requires noticing something that needs doing and being willing to act, which is a mindset available to absolutely anyone in the room.

Servant leadership inverts the usual mental picture of leadership. Instead of asking "how can people serve my goals and vision," it asks "how can I serve the people and the shared goal at the same time." This isn't about becoming passive or having no direction — it's about defining leadership success by what the group and its members gain, not by personal status.

Leading through service tends to build trust quickly and durably, because people can see the leader isn't primarily protecting their own position or reputation. A leader who visibly puts the group's success ahead of personal credit earns a kind of cooperation that purely authority-based leadership often struggles to generate, especially among peers of similar age or status.

Everyday service leadership doesn't require grand gestures. Noticing a struggling classmate and quietly offering help without being asked, organising something useful that nobody assigned you to organise, or simply giving credit to someone else rather than claiming it for yourself are all small acts of leadership that happen without any formal title attached.

Leadership through service is sustainable in a way that leadership through pure authority often isn't, particularly among peers rather than in a formal hierarchy. People generally follow authority because they have to; they follow service leadership because they want to — and the second kind of following tends to hold up under pressure far better than the first.

This doesn't mean service leaders never make hard, unpopular decisions — sometimes serving the group's real interest means saying something people don't want to hear. The distinction is in the underlying motive: is the hard decision genuinely for the group's benefit, or dressed-up self-interest? Honest self-reflection on that question is part of leading well.

b: Noticing a struggling classmate and offering to help, unprompted
Organising something useful nobody assigned you to organise
Giving credit to others rather than claiming it for yourself

p: Identifying and carrying out one genuine act of service leadership this week — something you weren't assigned to do, done because it was useful rather than because it would be noticed — is where this week's idea stops being theory and starts being a habit you're actually practising.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Walid Bial (16 years old) (Marrakech, Morocco)
p: Walid was elected as the president of his school’s youth club. He was very excited to be the leader. On his first day, he sat at the main desk, gave orders to the other students, and told them to clean up the club storage room while he checked his phone. The other students felt insulted, stopped working, and walked out of the room.
Walid was confused and went to his favorite teacher for advice. The teacher told him, "A true leader is not a boss who sits on a throne. A true leader is the person who grabs the broom first."

The next afternoon, Walid apologized to the group. He put on old clothes, grabbed a trash bag, and started scrubbing the dirty floor himself. Seeing their president working hard, the other students laughed, grabbed their brooms, and joined in happily. Walid learned that real leadership is not about power or status; it is about serving your team and leading by example.
Can you lead without having an official title? How?
Who is someone who leads through service, in your own life?
What is one way you could serve your class or community this month?
Identify and carry out one act of service leadership for your class or community this week.
Key takeaway: Understand leadership as service to others, not authority over them.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Identify and carry out one act of service leadership for your class or community this week.

units.title: Week 22: Networking
units.summary: Build genuine, respectful professional relationships (networking).
keyWords: Networking as relationship-building, not using people

p: Icebreaker: Who is someone you'd love to have a 15-minute conversation with, and why?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Walid Bial's technology-lab dream nearly died in a wall of confusing database errors — what actually unlocked it wasn't more solo studying, but one polite, specific email that turned a stranger into a monthly mentor.

Networking, done well, is not about using people for personal gain — it's about building genuine, curious relationships with people, some of whom happen to have more experience in an area you're interested in. The common negative image of networking (transactional, self-serving) describes networking done badly, not networking itself.

Walid's email worked because it was specific and modest in its ask: a clear introduction of who he was, a clear explanation of what he was working on, and a small, time-bound request (fifteen minutes, one piece of advice) rather than a vague or open-ended demand on someone's time. Specific, small asks are far easier for a busy person to say yes to than vague, large ones.

Most professionals are genuinely more willing to help young people than nervous teenagers tend to assume — as long as the approach is respectful, shows real effort, and doesn't feel entitled. A senior technology director doesn't owe a stranger fifteen minutes, but many people are glad to give it when asked well, particularly to someone clearly trying rather than expecting it.

A good outreach message generally follows a simple structure: briefly who you are, briefly what you're working on or curious about, a small and specific ask, and a thank-you regardless of the eventual answer. Messages that skip straight to a large, vague request ("can you help me with my career") are far less likely to get a response than ones with a clear, small ask.

Networking relationships that last require follow-through after the first conversation, not just a strong opening message. A brief thank-you note, an occasional update on progress, or simply staying in light touch turns a single fifteen-minute chat into an ongoing relationship — which is what actually happened between Walid and his mentor, well beyond that first conversation.

b: Who you are, briefly
What you're working on / curious about
A small, specific, time-bound ask
A thank-you regardless of the answer

p: Drafting a short, respectful outreach message this week — even without sending it yet — is genuinely useful practice, because the hardest part of networking for most people isn't the conversation itself, it's working up the courage to write and send the first message at all.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Ryan Ho (16 years old) (Singapore)
p: Ryan Ho loved coding video games, but he did not know anyone in the professional gaming industry. His school arranged a field trip to a massive local technology convention. While his friends stayed in a tight group laughing and eating free snacks, Ryan decided to practice his networking skills.

He felt shy, but he forced himself to walk up to a booth run by a professional game studio. He did not ask them for a job. Instead, he introduced himself politely, smiled, and asked the lead designer a simple question: "What is the biggest mistake young programmers make when starting out?"

The designer was impressed by Ryan's politeness and curiosity. They had a great five-minute chat, and the designer handed Ryan his business card, telling him to email his game projects for feedback. By stepping out of his comfort zone to build a polite connection, Ryan opened a huge door for his future career.
Why did Walid's polite, specific email work better than a generic request?
Who is someone you admire that you could respectfully reach out to?
What makes an introduction message feel genuine rather than 'salesy'?
Draft a short outreach message to someone you'd like advice from — you don't have to send it yet.
Key takeaway: Build genuine, respectful professional relationships (networking).
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.activity: Draft a short, polite outreach message to someone you'd like advice from (you do not have to send it).

units.title: Week 23: Cultural Intelligence
units.summary: Develop cultural intelligence and adapt communication across different backgrounds.

p: Icebreaker: Share one custom, food, or tradition from your own background that you're proud of.
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Working comfortably with people from a wide range of backgrounds is no longer a specialised skill reserved for international careers — group projects, online communities, and future workplaces routinely mix people from very different cultural contexts, and the skill of navigating that well is increasingly ordinary and necessary.

Cultural intelligence is the ability to work respectfully and effectively across different cultural backgrounds, which starts with a basic but often overlooked recognition: your own sense of "normal" — how to greet people, how directly to disagree, what counts as polite — is shaped by your own culture and isn't automatically shared by everyone else.

Curiosity works far better than assumption when encountering an unfamiliar cultural practice. Asking "can you tell me more about that?" invites someone to share and correct any misunderstanding directly; assuming you already understand a custom based on limited exposure risks getting it wrong and, worse, acting confidently on that wrong understanding.

Generalising an entire culture from a single example or a single person is a common and understandable mistake, but a mistake nonetheless. Any culture contains huge internal variation — by region, generation, religion, individual personality — and treating one person's behaviour as representative of an entire culture flattens a much more complex reality.

Being willing to be corrected, without becoming defensive, is a core part of cultural intelligence. Getting something wrong about an unfamiliar custom isn't a moral failure if the response is genuine curiosity and adjustment; treating a correction as an attack, and becoming defensive instead of listening, is what actually damages the relationship.

Cultural intelligence isn't just useful abroad — it applies within a single country or even a single classroom, where students can come from very different family backgrounds, religions, and traditions even while sharing a nationality. The same skill of respectful curiosity applies at every scale, from international travel to a conversation with a classmate.

b: Ask 'can you tell me about...' instead of assuming you already know
Notice when you're generalising a whole culture from one example
Be willing to be corrected without getting defensive

p: Interviewing someone from a different cultural background about a tradition that genuinely matters to them — and actually listening, rather than just waiting to share your own comparison — is this week's practical application of a skill that will keep mattering in every group this programme, and every group after it.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Amara Nwosu (13 years old) (Vancouver, Canada)
p: Amara moved from a small town in Nigeria to a highly diverse school in Vancouver, Canada. On her first day, she sat next to a classmate named Yuki, who had recently moved from Japan. At lunchtime, Amara offered Yuki a piece of her savory Nigerian meat pie. Yuki took it with both hands, bowed her head slightly, and did not make any sound while eating it.

Amara thought Yuki was being rude or cold because she did not shout "Thank you!" or jump up with excitement like her friends back home would. Instead of getting upset, Amara decided to learn about Yuki's background. She discovered that in Japanese culture, showing quiet respect and using two hands to accept a gift is a sign of deep gratitude.

The next day, Amara handed Yuki a snack using both of her hands and gave a gentle bow. Yuki’s face lit up with a massive, happy smile. Amara learned that cultural intelligence means understanding that people show respect and kindness in many different ways, and taking the time to learn those differences makes the world a much friendlier place.

How do you usually learn about a culture that isn't your own?

Key takeaway: Develop cultural intelligence and adapt communication across different backgrounds.

units.title: Quarter 2 Capstone — "The Leadership Challenge"
units.summary: Teams solve a community scenario together and present their response, assessed on communication, leadership, teamwork and problem-solving.

p: Icebreaker: What's one thing your team is genuinely proud of building together this quarter?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Eleven weeks of learning to speak clearly, listen actively, resolve conflict, negotiate, and lead through service all converge on one deliberately pressured challenge: solving a real community scenario as a team, under time.

"The Leadership Challenge" hands teams a community scenario to solve together, then assesses the response on four specific dimensions: communication, leadership, teamwork, and problem-solving — not just whether the final solution sounds good, but how visibly the team's process reflected everything practised since Week 13.

Strong teams for this capstone divide roles early, drawing on the team-roles thinking from Week 18, and communicate honestly the moment something isn't working, rather than letting a problem quietly fester until presentation day. Teams that skip this early role division often end up with duplicated effort in some areas and total gaps in others.

The negotiation and conflict-resolution skills from Weeks 19 and 20 tend to get tested directly during this capstone, since a real team solving a real scenario under time pressure will almost certainly disagree about something along the way. How that disagreement gets handled — calmly and structurally, or not — is itself part of what's being assessed, even if it's never stated explicitly.

A genuinely strong presentation for this capstone shows evidence of listening to each other throughout the process, not just a polished final pitch delivered by the most confident speaker while everyone else stays silent. Judges specifically notice whether a presentation reflects one voice or a whole team's coordinated thinking.

The community scenario itself should be treated as seriously as a real one, even though it's a structured exercise — a specific, workable, genuinely thought-through solution to the assigned scenario reflects the problem-solving muscle this whole quarter has been building, and demonstrates it more convincingly than a generic or hand-wavy response would.

ex.t: What a strong team presentation shows
b: Clear roles and shared ownership, not one person doing everything
Evidence of listening to each other during the process, not just the final polish
A specific, workable solution to the community scenario

units.title: Week 25: Critical Thinking
units.summary: Apply critical thinking to evaluate information and question assumptions.

p: Icebreaker: Share a claim you once believed that turned out to be false. How did you find out?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Not every confident-sounding claim is true, and not every claim that confirms what you already believe deserves to be accepted without question — which is exactly why critical thinking is a discipline you have to practise, not a trait some people simply have.

Critical thinking means questioning assumptions and evaluating evidence before accepting a claim as true — including, and especially, claims that already match what you want to believe, since those are the ones people are naturally least likely to scrutinise carefully. Confirmation bias, the tendency to favour information agreeing with existing beliefs, affects everyone, not just people who "fall for" misinformation.

A simple habit meaningfully improves how critically information gets evaluated: before sharing or fully accepting a claim, ask who said it, what evidence they've offered, and who might benefit from you believing it. That third question — who benefits — is often the most revealing, since motivated claims are common even when they're not outright false.

Weak reasoning has recognisable patterns worth learning to spot: an anecdote presented as universal proof ("it worked for my cousin, so it must work generally"), a source with an obvious reason to mislead, or a claim so neatly one-sided it seems designed to provoke agreement rather than genuine understanding of a complicated issue.

Critical thinking doesn't mean being cynical about everything or refusing to believe anything without exhaustive personal verification — that's neither practical nor actually more accurate. It means calibrating confidence to the actual strength of the evidence: holding strong claims to a higher standard of evidence than mundane, low-stakes ones.

Critical thinking applies to your own reasoning just as much as to external claims. Noticing when you've reached a conclusion quickly, and asking whether you'd accept the same quality of evidence from a claim you didn't already want to believe, is a genuinely uncomfortable but valuable habit to build.

b: Anecdote presented as universal proof ('it worked for my cousin, so it works')
A source with an obvious reason to mislead you
A claim that sounds too neat or too extreme to be balanced

p: Fact-checking a real claim you encounter online this week, using two independent sources rather than trusting the first confident-sounding result, turns critical thinking from an abstract virtue into a specific, repeatable habit — one that gets easier and faster the more often it's actually practised.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Emma Yang (16 years old) (New York City, USA)
p: Emma Yang spent a lot of time reading health articles online during her school breaks, but she soon noticed a very disturbing pattern. Dozens of websites were sharing medical stories and health advice that sounded completely fake, yet thousands of people were liking, sharing, and believing them without a second thought. Emma realized that people were blindly trusting whatever popped up on their screens because they lacked the tools to question the information. This dangerous trend made her realize that the internet needed a digital shield to help everyday citizens separate fact from fiction. Instead of just complaining about the issue, she decided to use her software programming skills to build an artificial intelligence app that could analyze online text and automatically detect fake news.

She spent months tucked away in her bedroom, typing thousands of lines of code and testing different algorithms. When she shared her idea with her high school classmates, some of them laughed and said it was completely impossible for a single teenager to outsmart professional internet liars. This skepticism did not stop Emma; instead, it pushed her to examine the problem even more closely from different angles. She collected thousands of verified real articles and compared them directly with known fake articles to find the hidden patterns in how fake news is written. Her intense research helped her train her app to look for exaggerated emotional words, unverified links, and anonymous authors that normal readers usually skip.

When major news stations heard about her invention, they invited her to speak live on television. The adult journalists on the panel asked Emma why anyone should trust a computer program written by a high school student instead of professional fact-checkers. Emma did not get defensive or nervous under the bright studio lights; she simply smiled and walked them through her logical process. She explained exactly how her code checked the source code of a website, verified the registration data of the link, and cross-referenced the claims with trusted scientific databases. By presenting clear, objective data instead of getting emotional, she completely changed the minds of the doubtful reporters and gained massive respect from top global tech executives.

Her successful presentation proved to teenagers everywhere that you do not have to accept everything you see, hear, or read at face value. Emma showed that critical thinking is not about arguing with people or being cynical; it is about slow, careful investigation and using logic to find the solid truth. Her app went on to help thousands of internet users check their sources before hitting the share button. By encouraging people to stop and ask hard questions, Emma proved that a sharp mind and a commitment to facts are the most powerful tools anyone can use to navigate the modern digital world.

How do you decide whether a source of information is trustworthy?
What assumption are you making about a problem you're currently facing?

Key takeaway: Apply critical thinking to evaluate information and question assumptions.

units.title: Week 26: Creative Thinking
units.summary: Generate original ideas using creative-thinking techniques.

p: Icebreaker: 60 seconds — how many uses can you think of for a paperclip?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Sixty seconds and a paperclip can reveal more about how creativity actually works than a lecture on the subject ever could — the exercise shows, immediately, that most people's first few ideas are obvious and their later ideas, forced out under a bit of pressure, are often far more original.

Creative thinking is a trainable skill, not a fixed gift reserved for a naturally artistic few. Divergent thinking — generating many possible ideas without judging them as they arrive — is the foundation of creativity; judgment and refinement come later, in a separate step, and mixing the two steps together too early is one of the most common ways creativity gets shut down.

Fear of looking silly is very often the biggest block to creative output in a group setting, more so than any genuine lack of imagination. People routinely censor their own ideas before saying them out loud, worried about a dismissive reaction — which means a huge portion of a group's actual creative potential never even makes it into the room.

Some of the most original ideas come from deliberately combining two unrelated things — a technique behind a huge number of inventions and creative breakthroughs throughout history. Forcing an unlikely combination (what would a library crossed with a vending machine look like?) often produces ideas a purely linear approach would never generate.

A genuine brainstorm has explicit rules worth stating out loud before starting: aim for quantity over quality at first, never judge or shoot down an idea mid-session, and actively build on other people's ideas rather than only offering your own. Groups that skip these rules tend to default back into cautious, obvious suggestions.

Quantity reliably produces quality, even though it feels counterintuitive. The first five ideas in almost any brainstorm tend to be the most obvious, easily-reached ones; the more interesting ideas tend to show up after those obvious options are exhausted and the mind is forced to reach further. Stopping at the first workable idea usually means missing the better ones that come after it.

b: Quantity over quality at first — aim for volume
No judging or shooting down ideas mid-brainstorm
Build on others' ideas rather than only offering your own

p: Brainstorming twenty ideas for a small everyday problem — with a genuine no-judging rule in place — and then picking a favourite, is this week's practice precisely because the discomfort of pushing past the first five obvious ideas is where real creative thinking actually starts.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Sibahle Zwane (11 years old) (Johannesburg, South Africa)
p: Sibahle Zwane absolutely loved mathematics, but his local school faced massive challenges because they did not have enough textbooks, calculators, or computers for the students. Many kids in his neighborhood felt discouraged by the lack of resources and found math classes incredibly boring. Instead of complaining about what he didn’t have, Sibahle decided to treat the entire world as his classroom. He found a very funny and highly unusual way to practice his mental skills by turning his daily walk to school into a massive math game. He began reading the random numbers printed on the license plates of passing cars and instantly multiplying or dividing them in his head before the vehicles drove out of sight.

This bizarre daily habit quickly turned Sibahle into a local legend in his neighborhood. Local shopkeepers and neighbors began standing outside their storefronts just to watch the young boy walk past and test his brain with giant math problems. A local resident eventually filmed a video of Sibahle multiplying complex three-digit numbers faster than an adult could type them into a digital smartphone. The video exploded in popularity online, gaining millions of views across the globe. Soon, representatives from a prestigious local university drove down to his neighborhood to meet him and were so amazed by his skills that they offered him a full academic scholarship for his future education.

The sudden fame did not change Sibahle's joyful attitude toward learning. One afternoon, a group of older students approached him with a smartphone calculator and challenged him to solve a massive math problem involving percentages and fractions. As a crowd gathered around to watch, Sibahle closed his eyes for a split second, danced on his toes, and shouted out the perfect answer before the smartphone screen could even finish calculating. The entire street burst into loud laughter and cheers, and the older boys shook his hand in complete disbelief. Sibahle proved to his community that creative thinking does not require expensive tools or fancy classrooms; it just requires an open imagination and the willingness to see learning opportunities in everyday objects.

His unique story inspired thousands of other children across South Africa to rethink how they viewed difficult school subjects. Sibahle showed his peers that math wasn't just a set of dry rules written in a textbook, but a living puzzle that could be played anywhere. By using his creativity to overcome a lack of resources, he opened doors for his future that his family never thought possible. He left a lasting lesson for young people everywhere that when you change the way you look at your surroundings, you can turn any ordinary street into a path toward success.

What blocks your creativity the most — fear of judgment, or fear of failure?
How can 'silly' ideas lead to genuinely good ones?

Key takeaway: Generate original ideas using creative-thinking techniques.

units.title: Week 27: Problem Solving
units.summary: Use a structured process to break down and solve real problems.

p: Icebreaker: Name a problem you solved recently, even a small one. How did you approach it?
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

The first fix that comes to mind for a problem is often aimed at a symptom, not the actual cause — which is why good problem-solving usually starts with more time spent understanding the problem than most people are naturally inclined to give it.

Defining the real problem clearly, before jumping to a solution, is the step most commonly skipped under time pressure — and skipping it is exactly what produces solutions that don't actually fix anything. "Students keep missing the deadline" sounds like a clear problem, but it's really a symptom description, not yet a diagnosis.

Root-cause thinking, often done by repeatedly asking "why," pushes past the first-layer symptom toward something actually fixable. "Students miss the deadline" → why? → "they don't know exactly when it is" → why? → "it was only announced verbally, once, in class." The real fix — posting it somewhere permanent — only becomes obvious after that deeper digging.

Testing a small, rough version of a solution before committing fully saves significant time and reveals flaws early, while they're still cheap to fix. A rough, five-minute test of an idea often reveals a problem that a week of careful, polished planning would have missed entirely, simply because the rough test exposes the idea to reality faster.

Problem-solving benefits from generating multiple possible solutions before picking one, rather than committing to the very first workable idea. The first solution that comes to mind is rarely the best one available — it's simply the fastest one to think of, which are not the same quality.

Some problems are genuinely worth reframing rather than solving as originally stated. A problem framed as "how do we get more students to attend" might be better reframed as "why don't students want to attend" — the second framing often points toward a more useful and different set of solutions than the first.

b: Symptom: 'students keep missing the deadline' → Why? → 'they don't know when it is' → Why? → 'it's only announced verbally once'
Real fix: post it somewhere permanent, not just repeat it louder

p: Choosing one real problem around you, defining it clearly using the root-cause approach, and sketching a possible solution turns problem-solving from a vague virtue into a specific process you've actually walked through — one that gets faster and more natural each time it's used again.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Reyhan Jamalova (17 years old) (Baku, Azerbaijan)
p: Reyhan Jamalova grew up in a city that frequently experienced intense, heavy rainstorms that caused major disruptions. These massive downpours often overwhelmed the local electrical grid, leading to sudden blackouts that left hundreds of families sitting in the dark without heating or internet. While most people simply complained about the bad weather and waited for the power company to fix the lines, Reyhan began to look at the falling rain differently. She wondered why the city was letting millions of gallons of fast-moving water go to waste when that kinetic energy could potentially be captured and turned into clean electricity for the community. When she shared her idea with her school science teacher, he shook his head and told her the concept was far too complicated to build without an expensive laboratory.

Reyhan refused to let a lack of money stop her from trying to solve the energy problem. She spent her weekends searching through local junkyards and her family’s garage, gathering old plastic plumbing tubes, broken toy motors, and scraps of copper wire. She set up a temporary workspace in her backyard and spent months building a unique, mechanical device that she named Rainergy. Her plan was simple: the device would collect pouring rainwater from roof gutters, funnel it down a narrow tube to increase its speed, and use that fast water to spin a tiny toy motor that generated electrical currents. Her goal was to create a cheap, portable system that poor families could easily set up outside their homes during storms to keep their lights on.

However, her very first public test in her backyard turned into a complete disaster. A sudden blast of storm wind caught the lightweight plastic frame of her prototype, smashing it against the ground and breaking her carefully soldered copper wires into pieces. Water leaked all over her tools, and her device lay ruined in the mud while the rain kept pouring down. Reyhan did not cry or throw her tools away in frustration; instead, she laughed at the messy situation, dried off her hands, and carried the broken pieces back to her desk. She used thicker plastic tubes and stronger glue to rebuild the frame, making it tough enough to withstand severe weather.

The next time a major storm hit the city, Reyhan stood under an umbrella in her backyard and watched the water rush through her newly rebuilt device. Within seconds, the tiny LED light bulb attached to the generator flickered to life and shone with a brilliant, steady glow. Her persistent problem-solving skills had successfully turned a frustrating weather disaster into a useful source of clean, free energy. Reyhan proved to teenagers worldwide that real problem solving is not about getting everything right on the first try; it is about studying your failures, fixing your mistakes, and refusing to quit until you find a practical answer to the challenge in front of you.
What is a real problem in your school or community that bothers you?
What is the real root cause, versus the surface symptom?
What would a first, small test of a solution look like?
Choose one real problem around you, define it clearly, and sketch one possible solution.
Key takeaway: Use a structured process to break down and solve real problems.
Self-rating (1–5): How confident do I feel applying this skill right now?

units.title: Week 28: Decision Making
units.summary: Use a simple framework to make better decisions under uncertainty.

p: Icebreaker: Describe a decision you're currently torn about (nothing too private).
Quick round: What did I practise from last week? What was difficult? What did I learn? How has this changed me so far?

Every day involves dozens of small decisions made almost automatically, and a handful of larger ones that genuinely deserve more careful thought — knowing which is which, and having a simple process ready for the second kind, is what "good decision-making" actually means in practice.

Good decisions generally balance three things: the facts of the situation, personal values, and realistic consequences — not just gut feeling in the moment, and not just what a friend or family member happens to suggest. Relying on only one of these three — pure feeling, or pure logic with no regard for values — tends to produce decisions that don't hold up well.

Listing real options, rather than the first two that come to mind, often reveals a better path than the obvious binary choice a decision initially seems to present. Many decisions that feel like "A or B" actually have a reasonable C, D, or even a combination of A and B, that only becomes visible once you deliberately look for more than two options.

Weighing each option against your own stated values — not against what would impress someone else, or what feels easiest in the moment — keeps a decision honest. A decision framework works best when it's genuinely personal, connected to what actually matters to the person making the choice, rather than a generic checklist applied without reflection.

Considering the realistic worst-case outcome of each option, rather than either an overly optimistic or overly catastrophic version, keeps decision-making grounded. Most decisions aren't actually as high-stakes as they feel in the moment — and clearly naming the real worst case (not the imagined worst case) often reduces unnecessary anxiety around the choice.

Avoiding a decision is itself a decision, and usually the one with the least control over the eventual outcome. Decisions left unmade by default don't disappear — they get made anyway, just passively, by whatever happens next rather than by deliberate choice. Recognising this makes "I'll decide later" a more honest, and often less appealing, option.

b: List your real options (not just the two obvious ones)
For each, ask: does this fit my values? What's the realistic best/worst case?
Decide, then commit — don't keep relitigating after you've chosen

p: Applying this week's framework to a real decision you're currently facing — not a hypothetical one, but something actually undecided in your life right now — is what turns decision-making from a nice idea into a process you trust enough to actually use under real pressure.

sections.h: This Week's Story — Autumn Peltier (17 years old) (Ontario, Canada)
p: Autumn Peltier found herself facing a massive personal dilemma that kept her awake for days. Because of her incredible work as an environmental activist, she received an official invitation to fly across the world and give a major speech about clean water protection at a massive international conference. However, when she looked at her calendar, she realized with a heavy heart that the conference fell on the exact same weekend as her high school basketball championship game. Autumn had practiced with her basketball team all year, and her teammates were counting on her to help them win the regional trophy. She felt completely torn down the middle between her loyalty to her friends and her duty to her community.

To help her navigate this stressful situation, Autumn decided to step back from her emotions and make a logical list of the long-term impact of both choices. She realized that while the basketball game would be an absolute blast, the excitement would only last for one single afternoon. On the other hand, her speech at the global conference would be heard by powerful world leaders who had the direct authority to create new laws protecting clean drinking water for thousands of indigenous children. By weighing the short-term fun against the long-term value, she made the incredibly mature decision to pass up the championship game and board the plane to the conference.

When the day arrived to tell her basketball coach and her teammates about her final choice, Autumn’s stomach was full of nervous knots because she was terrified that they would think she was selfish. Instead of getting angry, her coach gathered the entire team in the gym and handed Autumn a basketball that every single player had signed with encouraging messages for her trip. As Autumn walked out onto the massive international stage a few days later, she felt a wave of fear looking at the crowd of adults in expensive suits. She took a deep breath, pictured the signed basketball in her mind, and delivered a powerful speech that brought the entire auditorium to its feet for a standing ovation.

Her viral speech helped raise thousands of dollars for clean water filters, proving that her difficult decision had achieved exactly what she hoped. Autumn learned that good decision making does not mean choosing the easiest path or trying to make absolutely everyone happy at the same time. It means aligning your choices with your deepest values and having the courage to stick to your purpose, even when it means missing out on temporary fun. Her journey showed teenagers everywhere that making thoughtful choices today is the only way to build a meaningful impact for tomorrow.
